learningObjective: Distinguish the situations in which recomputation (activation checkpointing) is a net win from those where it is not.
stem: Activation recomputation (a.k.a. gradient / activation checkpointing) trades extra forward FLOPs at backward time for reduced peak activation memory. Which of the following statements about the trade-off are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Recomputation is a net win when the peak activation memory (before checkpointing) exceeds the device budget and prevents a larger batch size or sequence length that would raise end-to-end throughput more than the recompute FLOPs cost.
Recomputing a cheap operator (e.g., elementwise activation) whose activation tensor is large is generally favorable, since the FLOPs added are small relative to the memory saved.
Recomputing an operator whose forward is compute-bound and whose activation is small (e.g., a heavy GEMM with a tiny output) is usually favorable, because the compiler gains ILP.
Recomputation changes the mathematical output of the forward and backward passes; users must accept a small accuracy drop.
Selective (per-op) recomputation policies can outperform whole-block checkpointing by choosing to recompute only the ops with the highest memory-per-FLOPs ratio.

explanation: A is the fundamental rationale (memory pressure enabling more batching / longer context often more than offsets the recompute cost). B is the classic favorable case: cheap op with big activation (e.g., GELU, dropout) is a prime candidate to recompute. E captures the observation behind selective checkpointing schemes: not every op has the same memory-per-FLOPs ratio, so a targeted policy dominates uniform block checkpointing. C is the opposite of the favorable case — recomputing an expensive op with a small activation adds a lot of FLOPs for little memory saving. D is wrong: recomputation is semantics-preserving; it produces the same values that would have been cached.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: the standard motivation is unlocking larger batches / longer contexts that raise throughput.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: high memory-per-FLOPs ops are ideal to recompute.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: describes the anti-pattern (recompute an expensive op with a small activation).
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: recomputation is exact (modulo hardware nondeterminism); no accuracy change is expected.
optionExplanations.E: Correct: selective recomputation is a well-known refinement over uniform checkpointing.

assumptions: Recomputation reruns the forward function deterministically enough to reproduce the cached value.
The end-to-end throughput metric accounts for both FLOPs and memory-limited batch/context growth.
nonImplications: Does not imply recomputation is always a net win; when the model already fits with headroom, it only adds compile complexity and FLOPs.
Does not imply the memory saved is exactly the sum of avoided activation sizes; buffer reuse interactions can dilute the benefit.
